posts.body:
Welcome aboard.

**forum/ui** is a forum interface kit: every page you see here is a template built from the same small set of components.

A few things to try first:

- Browse the forums and open a thread
- Leave a message on somebody's profile
- Start a conversation from the inbox

> Everything you post is stored in the demo database, so it survives a reload.

Have a look at the [component playground](/ui) if you want to see the pieces in isolation.
Glad to finally see this live. The post layout reads really well on a phone.
The red accent on near black is doing a lot of work. Love it.
First time posting here. Is there a rule about signatures?
Signatures are a permission: you can get one in the credits shop, and some ranks include it.
Bookmarked the playground. The editor is nicer than I expected.
Small request: could usernames of staff be highlighted in thread lists too?
Noted, adding it to the list for the next changelog.

## What changed

1. The composer is now a rich text editor with a toolbar
2. Phones get a bottom navigation bar
3. Profile walls support comments and likes

The editor still stores plain Markdown, for example:

```md
**bold**, *italic*, `code` and [links](https://example.com)
```

Report anything odd in the suggestions forum.
The Markdown export is a great call. Makes posts portable.
Bottom navigation feels native. Thumb friendly at last.
Found one issue: nested lists lose a level when I paste them. Will open a thread.
Thanks, tag me when you do and I will reproduce it.

We are moving the demo to a new host on **Sunday at 03:00 UTC**. Expect about ten minutes of downtime.

Nothing will be lost.
Thanks for the heads up.

Just wanted to say it. Supporting one theme properly beats supporting two halfway.

If anything, I would ask for a *slightly* lighter card surface on low quality panels.
We tested three surface levels. The current one won on OLED, which is most phones here.
Agreed with the choice. Fewer tokens, fewer bugs.
Fair enough. Maybe a contrast setting someday.
Could we get a visible list of shortcuts? I only found out about `Ctrl + B` by accident.

They follow the usual conventions:

- `Ctrl + B` bold
- `Ctrl + I` italic
- `Ctrl + Z` undo

A cheat sheet is a good idea though.
Perfect, thank you.

Weekly check in. I am rebuilding my template store checkout and trying not to rewrite everything else along the way.

What about you?
Migrating a queue worker from polling to notifications. Boring, satisfying.
A 32 by 32 icon set for a note taking app. 140 icons down, 60 to go.
Routing a new any percent run. Found a clip that saves four seconds.
Finishing my first portfolio page. Flexbox finally clicked.
Brand refresh for a bakery. The client wants the logo *bigger*, obviously.
Classic. Good luck with the bakery.
For me it was a monitor arm. Freed half the desk and fixed my posture in one go. What was yours?
A proper desk lamp with a warm setting. Night sessions hurt less.
Wrist rest. Should have bought one years ago.
A second hand drawing tablet stand. Not glamorous, used daily.
I get more done at home but I miss the whiteboard arguments. Curious how everyone here splits it.
Home for deep work, office for planning days. Two days in is my limit.
Coffee shops, oddly. Background noise helps me sketch.

I keep a tiny palette for anything that sits on a near black background:

- One saturated accent, used rarely
- Three greys with a hint of blue
- Pure white only for text

> If everything glows, nothing does.

Happy to share the swatches if anyone wants them.
Yes please. The quote should be printed on a poster.
This is exactly the restraint my templates need.
Would love a thread on how you pick the greys.
Will write it up this weekend.

Round two after client feedback. Wordmark is hand drawn, the wheat mark is new.

Be honest, I can take it.
The wordmark is lovely. The wheat mark fights it at small sizes, try dropping two grains.
Check the spacing between the R and the Y, it opens up on the second line.

Three things that mattered more than raw execution:

1. **Buffer inputs** during transitions
2. Skip optional dialog with a damage boost
3. Practise the last split first

The third one sounds silly and works every time.
Practising the ending first is such a good tip for nerves.
Do you keep the route in a spreadsheet or a notes file?
Plain text file in a repo. Diffing routes is underrated.
Looking for something relaxing with no timers and no fail states. Farming, building, puzzles, all welcome.
Anything with a good fishing minigame gets my vote.
I have been playing a little train puzzle game on my phone, perfect for this.
Same experience here. Progressive enhancement for free is the underrated part.
How do you handle validation errors without client state?
Return them from the action and read them with `useActionState`. One hook, done.
Saving this thread. I was about to build an API for a contact form.
Please do not build an API for a contact form.

My cards look fine on desktop but there is a horizontal scrollbar on my phone. I use `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 300px)`.

What am I missing?
Fixed pixel tracks cannot shrink. Try `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(min(100%, 18rem), 1fr))`.
And start from one column, then add columns at wider breakpoints. Mobile first saves you from this whole class of bug.
That fixed it. Thank you both!
Prompt, font, colours. Screenshots welcome, dotfiles even more so.
Stock shell, one alias file, a mono font with ligatures turned **off**.
Mine is mostly timers and split tracking. No regrets.

To celebrate 200 sales I am giving away three licenses.

Reply with the one component you rebuild in every project. Winners picked on Friday.
The data table. Every single time.
Navigation bars. I have made so many.
Empty states. Nobody budgets time for them.
Date pickers, and I regret it each time.
Form field wrappers with label, hint and error.
Hi all, I am Tobi. I am learning web development after work and this place looked friendly. Tips for a beginner are welcome!
Welcome, Tobi. Build small things and finish them.
Welcome! The coding lounge is beginner friendly, ask anything.
Hello and welcome. Share your portfolio when it is ready.
Marlowe here. I read forums like this for years without an account. Figured it was time.
Welcome out of the shadows.

A set of 200 icons drawn on a 16 pixel grid.

- SVG and PNG
- Three weights
- Free updates

Price is **29 credits**. Message me for a sample pack.
Bought the previous set, quality is consistent. Vouch.
Do you include the source files?
Yes, the source file with all artboards is included.
Tracks contributions, dividends and allocation drift. No macros, works anywhere.
The allocation drift chart alone is worth it.

Logo, palette, type system and a one page guideline. Two rounds of revisions included.

Turnaround is about two weeks.
Saffron did my store branding. Clear process and on time.
Do you take small budgets for student projects?
Sometimes, send me a message with details.
Need 12 simple line illustrations, dark background friendly. Budget is flexible for the right style.
Sent you a message with samples.

Three changes that doubled my rate in a year:

1. Quote per project, never per hour
2. Send three options, the middle one is what you want
3. Say the number and then **stop talking**

The silence is uncomfortable. It also works.
Number two is so effective it feels like cheating.
Works for contracting too. Thanks for writing this up.
Saving this for when I get my first client.
The middle option trick is just anchoring, and anchoring is undefeated.
I pay 30 percent to affiliates on my templates. It brings in about a fifth of revenue. Curious what rates others see.
A fifth of revenue at that rate is healthy. I would not change it.

Unpopular opinion: most people do not have a selection problem, they have a sizing problem.

> Size so that being wrong is boring.

A simple rule I use is never more than 2 percent of the portfolio at risk on a single idea.
Boring is the goal. Good post.
Reminder to everyone that nothing here is financial advice.
Being wrong is rarely boring for me, so I clearly size badly.
I moved everything into a single global index fund a year ago. Results: fewer decisions, better sleep, and returns that match the market, which was the point.
This is the least exciting and most convincing thread in this section.
Same approach here. Automation does the rest.

The autumn update went out this morning. Nothing you have posted has moved or changed, but a few things around your posts have. Here is the short version, followed by the details for anyone who wants them.

## What is new

- **Reactions.** Six of them, under every post and every wall post. One reaction per member per post, and you can change your mind.
- **Profile walls.** Every profile now has a wall. Post a status on your own, or leave a note on someone else's.
- **Thread prefixes.** Question, Guide, Debate, Showcase, Selling, Buying, News and Solved. Pick one when you start a thread, or leave it empty.
- **Four new boards.** News Around the World, International Lounge, Templates & Themes and Side Hustles. They are empty right now, so the first thread in each is yours to take.

## What we changed quietly

1. Search now looks inside code blocks.
2. Long tables scroll inside the post instead of stretching the page.
3. Notification emails are grouped: one message per thread per day, not one per reply.

## A note on prefixes

Prefixes are there to help people scan a board, not to decorate titles. Please do not type your own tags in square brackets any more; moderators will tidy those up as they find them.

> If you asked a question and somebody answered it, switch the prefix to Solved. It takes two seconds and saves the next person ten minutes.

If something looks broken, reply here with the page and what you expected to see. Kestrel and I are reading everything this week.
Moderation note to go with this: the marketplace boards only accept Selling and Buying prefixes. If your thread is a question about selling, it belongs in Freelancing or General Discussion.
New here, so I have nothing to compare it to, but the wall is a nice touch. Is there a limit on how long a status can be, or will it happily take a whole essay from me?

Found one: on a narrow phone the reaction picker opens off the left edge of the screen when the post is the first one on the page. Everything else has been smooth. The grouped emails alone were worth the update.

> on a narrow phone the reaction picker opens off the left edge of the screen

Fixed as of ten minutes ago, thank you for the precise report. The picker now flips to whichever side has room.

Marlowe: statuses stop at 500 characters. Essays go in threads, where people can find them later.

Hi again, everyone. I'm Tobi, I live in Lagos and I work in logistics during the day. In the evenings I'm teaching myself HTML and CSS, mostly by rebuilding pages I like and then finding out why mine look wrong.

So far I can centre things (most of the time), I understand the box model, and flexbox finally makes sense. Grid still feels like magic I haven't earned yet.

I'd like to build a small site for my sister's tailoring business before the end of the year. If anyone has advice on what to learn next and what to ignore for now, I'm listening.
Welcome. Coding Lounge is the place for the "why does mine look wrong" questions. Post the smallest example that still shows the problem and you will usually have an answer within the hour.

Welcome, Tobi. A real project with a deadline is the best teacher there is, so the tailoring site is a great plan.

My suggested order, for what it's worth:

1. Grid for page layout, flexbox for the things inside it.
2. Custom properties for colours and spacing, so you change a value in one place.
3. Responsive images with `srcset`, because a tailoring site will be mostly photos.

Ignore preprocessors, animation libraries and anything with a build step until the site is live. You won't miss them.
Welcome! When you get to the tailoring site, post a draft in Graphic Discussion. Fabric photography is tricky to design around and I'm happy to give the layout a once-over.
Thank you all, this is a warmer welcome than I expected. Ada, I've written your list on a sticky note above my desk. Grid starts tonight.

Can confirm this is the number one support request I get for dashboard templates. Someone drops a twelve-column data table into a card and the whole shell blows out.

I now ship every layout with `minmax(0, 1fr)` by default and wrap tables in a scrolling container. Support emails about "the sidebar disappeared" went from weekly to roughly never.

Good write-up. One small disagreement: I would not dismiss `overflow: hidden` completely. For cards where nothing interactive touches the edge, it is one declaration and it also contains floats and margins. Agreed that it is the wrong default for anything containing a focusable element.

> For cards where nothing interactive touches the edge, it is one declaration

Fair. My objection is mostly that "nothing interactive touches the edge" is true on the day you write it and false six months later when someone adds a button. `overflow: clip` with `overflow-clip-margin` is a decent middle ground if you want containment without losing outlines.
This is exactly what happened to my practice page last night. I had a long link in a paragraph and thought I had broken grid itself. Added `minmax(0, 1fr)` and the scrollbar is gone. Thank you!
I am not a developer and I understood this from start to finish, which I did not expect. The blockquote in the middle did most of the work. Bookmarked for the day I finally build my own site.

I sold a small side project last month and have a sum sitting in a savings account that is larger than anything I have invested in one go before. The plan was always a broad, low-cost, global index fund. The open question is how to get the money in.

This is a debate thread, not advice. I am not qualified to tell anyone what to do with their money, and neither is anyone replying.

## The case for investing it all at once

- Markets have risen in more years than they have fallen, so money that is waiting has historically missed more gains than losses.
- It is one decision. No calendar, no temptation to "wait for a better week".
- Costs are lower if your broker charges per order.

## The case for spreading it out

- If the market drops sharply the month after you invest, you will feel it, and feelings are what make people sell at the bottom.
- Spreading over six or twelve months caps the regret in either direction.
- It matches how most of us invest anyway, out of monthly income.

> The best plan is the one you will still be following in a bad year.

## What I am leaning towards

Twelve equal instalments, automated, so I cannot interfere. For anyone who wants to do the same and likes their numbers to add up exactly, this is the helper I wrote to split an amount without losing a cent to rounding:

```ts
function instalments(total: number, months: number): number[] {
  const cents = Math.round(total * 100);
  const base = Math.floor(cents / months);
  const remainder = cents - base * months;

  return Array.from({ length: months }, (_, i) =>
    (base + (i < remainder ? 1 : 0)) / 100
  );
}

instalments(10000, 12); // four payments of 833.34, then eight of 833.33
```

So: if you have been in this position, which way did you go, and would you do it again?

All at once, two years ago, after a good launch month. It dropped about eight percent within weeks and I felt sick. It recovered, I did nothing, and today I would not be able to tell you which approach would have come out ahead without looking it up. Which I think is the point.

Freelancer perspective: my income is lumpy, so everything I invest is effectively a small lump sum at a random time. I stopped thinking about timing years ago because I simply never had the option.

The one thing I would add to your list is the emergency fund. Before any of it goes in, I keep six months of expenses untouched. A quiet quarter should never force you to sell.

Polite disagreement with the twelve months. If the argument for spreading is psychological, three or four instalments buy you most of the comfort. A full year is long enough that you are really just holding cash and calling it a strategy.

> A full year is long enough that you are really just holding cash and calling it a strategy.

That stings a little because it is accurate. I picked twelve because it is a round number, which is not a reason. Six is probably the honest compromise between what the history suggests and what I know about my own nerves.

I know nothing about funds but I do know about tilting. In speedrunning, the run after a bad reset is always worse because you are playing angry. Automating it so you cannot touch it sounds like the investing version of "never reset on emotion". I would trust that instinct.

Beginner question, and apologies if it is too basic for this board: when people say "low-cost", what number are they actually looking at? I see fees listed as tiny percentages and cannot tell whether the difference between them matters.

Not too basic at all. The number is the ongoing charge, shown as a yearly percentage of what you hold. The difference looks trivial and is not, because it is taken every year from the whole balance rather than from the gains.

A rough way to feel it:

- 0.2% a year on 10,000 is 20 a year.
- 1.5% a year on the same amount is 150 a year.
- Over decades the gap compounds, because every fee paid is also money that never gets the chance to grow.

Broad index funds tend to sit at the low end. Check the fund's own fact sheet rather than a comparison site, and check what your broker charges on top.

First thread on the new board, so I'll try to set a decent example. Harbor is the dashboard template I have been building since spring, and version 1.0 is ready.

**What you get**

- 42 screens: analytics, billing, team management, settings, onboarding and a full set of empty and error states
- Light and dark themes driven by custom properties, no duplicated stylesheets
- 60+ components with keyboard support and visible focus styles
- Plain HTML and CSS plus a typed component version, same markup in both

**Pricing:** 39 for a single project, 99 for unlimited projects. Both include a year of updates. Refunds within 14 days, no questions.

Happy to answer anything here. Screenshots and a live preview are linked from my profile.

Looks very clean. Two questions before I recommend it to a client: does the typed version render on the server without layout shift when the theme is dark, and are the charts part of the template or a separate dependency?

Good questions, both.

1. Yes. The theme is set from a cookie before first paint, with a tiny inline script as a fallback, so there is no flash of the wrong theme.
2. The charts are plain SVG components that ship with the template. No charting dependency, which also means they are fairly basic: line, bar, area and a sparkline. If you need more than that, the containers are sized to drop anything else in.

In April I set myself a slightly silly goal: draw an interface icon every day, at two sizes, by hand, on the pixel grid. No vectors scaled down, no automatic hinting. Yesterday I placed the last pixel of icon number 240, which makes 480 glyphs in total. This is the write-up.

## What I built

- 240 icons, each drawn separately at 16 px and 24 px
- 12 categories: navigation, files, media, commerce, weather, devices, editing, social, maps, charts, status and a "misc" drawer I'm not proud of
- A 9-colour palette with a light and a dark variant of every icon
- A contact sheet and a naming scheme that finally makes sense

## What I learned

1. **The 24 px version is not the 16 px version with more pixels.** At 16 you are drawing a symbol; at 24 you are drawing an object. They need different decisions.
2. **Diagonals are the enemy.** A 45 degree line is fine. Anything else needs manual clean-up, pixel by pixel.
3. **Consistency beats cleverness.** A dull icon that matches its neighbours looks better in a toolbar than a brilliant one that doesn't.

> Zoom out before you judge it. Nobody will ever see your icon at 800 percent.

## The boring part that saved me

Halfway through I discovered that eleven icons existed at one size only. Since then, this runs before every export:

```bash
for file in src/16/*.png; do
  name="$(basename "$file")"
  [ -f "src/24/$name" ] || echo "missing 24px: $name"
done
```

## What is next

The set becomes volume 3 of my icon packs later this month. Before that I'd like honest feedback on the weather category, which I have redrawn three times and still don't trust. Contact sheets are in the attachments.

This is gorgeous work, and the write-up is as good as the icons. On weather: the cloud shapes are lovely, but the sun rays at 16 px read as a gear to me. Try four rays instead of eight and give them a one-pixel gap from the disc.
The controller icon in the devices set has the exact shoulder button shape of the pad I grew up with and I felt that in my soul. Take my money when volume 3 is out.
I don't know enough to give feedback, but I have a question. Why draw two sizes by hand? Would it not be faster to draw the big one and let the software shrink it?

Good question, Tobi, and it is the whole reason the project exists.

When software shrinks a 24 px drawing to 16 px, every line that used to sit neatly on a pixel now lands between pixels. The software blends them, and you get a soft grey smudge where a crisp line used to be. At small sizes the eye notices immediately.

Drawing each size by hand means every stroke sits exactly on the grid. It is three times the work and it is the only way I know to get icons that look sharp on an ordinary screen.

Saffron: four rays with a gap. Trying it tonight, thank you.
Featuring this on the front page for the week. This is what the Showcase prefix was made for.

39:47. After three months, 612 attempts and one controller that did not survive, I finally have a sub-40 run of the little cave platformer I have been obsessed with since summer.

The time save was not where I expected. I spent weeks drilling the hard skip in the third area, which saves eleven seconds when it works and loses forty when it doesn't. What actually got me under was boring: cleaner menus, a safer route through the flooded section, and not resetting every time the first boss took one extra cycle.

Next goal is 38:30. I'm told that is where it stops being fun. We'll see.
Congratulations! 612 attempts is a number I recognise from redrawing a single umbrella icon. Did you keep splits for all of them?
"The time save was in the boring parts" is the most transferable lesson I have read on this forum. It is true of slow test suites and of budgets too. Well played.

Every single one, in a spreadsheet that is now frankly embarrassing. The chart of my average over time is nearly flat for six weeks and then falls off a cliff the week I stopped going for the skip. I should frame it.

Brand identity project, fixed fee, contract says two rounds of revisions. We are now past the third, which I did as a goodwill gesture, and this morning I got an email that starts with "one last quick thing" and contains a list of nine.

The client is lovely, pays on time and has already referred me to someone. I don't want to sour that. I also can't keep working for free, and I suspect the list of nine will become a list of fourteen.

How do you raise it without sounding like you are waving the contract in their face?

Been there with custom template work. What works for me is replying as if the paid route is the obvious, friendly default:

> Happy to take these on. We've used the rounds included in the project, so I'll put this list through as a small add-on. It comes to X and I can have it back to you by Friday. Shall I go ahead?

No apology, no mention of the contract, a price and a date. Most clients say yes within the hour. The ones who don't usually cut the list to the two things they actually care about.

From the other side of the table, as someone who has hired designers for book covers: I have been that client, and I honestly did not realise I was over the limit until someone told me. A clear, friendly message like the one above would have been a relief, not an insult.

Agree with both. The mistake was the free third round, not the email you are about to send. Goodwill that is not named as goodwill just becomes the new baseline. Next time, do the favour and put it on the invoice as a line with a zero next to it.

Update: I sent almost exactly Driftwood's wording yesterday. Reply came back in twenty minutes: "Of course, go ahead, sorry, I lost count." The list shrank from nine to five on its own.

The zero-value invoice line is going into my template today. Thank you, all three of you.

Opening this board with a format I intend to keep: one thread a week, short items, no hot takes. If you have something for next week's edition, reply here or leave it on my wall.

## Web platform

- Browser vendors have published their shared compatibility priorities for the coming year. Layout features dominate the list again, which is good news for anyone who read [the grid overflow guide](/threads/29) and wants fewer workarounds.
- A widely used open-source typeface family has shipped a variable version with an optical size axis. One file instead of twelve.
- The accessibility guidelines working group has opened its next draft for public comment. The focus appearance criteria are the part most worth reading.

## Money and markets

- Several payment providers are moving to weekly payouts by default for new seller accounts in a number of regions. If you sell digital goods, check your dashboard before you plan your month.
- Fund fee cuts continued this quarter, with a few broad index trackers lowering their ongoing charges again. There is a good discussion of what those percentages mean in [the lump sum debate](/threads/30).

## Makers

1. Registration has opened for the winter edition of the big online game jam. Theme is announced on the first evening, as usual.
2. A long-running pixel art community has published its yearly palette competition results. Sixteen colours, and the winning entry manages to make brown look exciting.
3. Closer to home: reactions, walls and prefixes arrived here last week. Details in [the changelog](/threads/27).

> A roundup is only useful if it is shorter than the things it links to.

That is the week. Corrections welcome.
Useful format, please do keep it. The payout change caught me by surprise last month; a monthly budget looks quite different when the money arrives in four pieces.
Pinned for the week. If this becomes a habit, we will add a roundup archive to the board description.

I'm putting together a small collection of nine short stories, all set in the same seaside town, and I need a cover. Print and e-book, standard paperback size.

What I have in mind is limited colour, slightly retro, with one strong image rather than a collage. I have a budget of around 400 and I'm not in a hurry: end of November would be perfect. I'd need the right to use the art on the cover and in promotion, and I'm glad to credit you prominently.

If this sounds like your kind of thing, reply here or send me a message with two or three samples.

Limited colour and one strong image is very much my corner. I work in pixels, which is unusual for a book cover, but it prints beautifully at high scale and it certainly stands out on a shelf. Sending you three samples now, including a harbour scene I drew last winter.

Not pitching for the illustration, Pixelmonk is the right call for that brief. But a cover is half picture and half lettering, so make sure the title typography is part of the agreement, or have someone set it properly afterwards. Happy to do the type if you two end up working together.
One addition: `dvh` follows the visible viewport on phones, where the address bar slides in and out. If you want a fallback for older browsers, put `min-height: 100vh;` on the line before it.

It works! Footer is at the bottom on the contact page and still behaves on the gallery page. And I recognised `minmax(0, 1fr)` from Ada's guide, so I even understand why it is there. Changing the prefix to Solved.

Twelve months ago I put my first dashboard template up for sale while working a full-time job. This month it paid my rent for the first time. I promised myself I would write the honest version when that happened, so here it is.

## The numbers, roughly

- Months 1 to 3: a handful of sales, mostly to people who already knew me
- Months 4 to 8: slow and steady, around one sale every two days
- Months 9 to 12: about three sales a day after the second product launched

It was never a hockey stick. It was a staircase, and each step was a specific thing I did.

## What worked

1. **A free, useful slice.** I gave away the login and settings screens. People who used them came back for the rest.
2. **Writing about problems, not the product.** One article about table overflow brought in more buyers than every launch post combined.
3. **Simple licences.** I started with five tiers and nobody could work out which one they needed. This is the entire configuration now:

```json
{
  "single": { "price": 39, "projects": 1, "updates": "1 year" },
  "unlimited": { "price": 99, "projects": null, "updates": "1 year" }
}
```

## What did not

- Discount codes. They trained people to wait for the next one.
- A community chat for buyers. It was lovely, and it turned into unpaid support at eleven at night.
- Building the features that the loudest three customers asked for. None of the three renewed.

> Support is part of the product. If you would not want to answer the question forever, do not ship the feature.

## If you are starting now

Pick something small enough to finish in six weekends, sell it before it is perfect, and keep the day job longer than feels necessary. The calm of not needing the next sale is what lets you make good decisions about it.

Ask me anything. I'll answer with real figures where I can.

Thank you for writing the staircase version instead of the highlight reel. Question on the licences: when you went from five tiers to two, did revenue per sale drop? I would have guessed the middle tiers were doing quiet work.

This board is new and empty, so here is an easy one to start it off. We are clearly spread across a lot of time zones; I see replies arrive at what must be three in the morning for somebody.

Tell us where you are and what a normal working day looks like. When do you start, what is lunch, what does the commute involve, when do you finally sit down to your own projects?

I'll go first: small coastal town, I write from six until nine before the day job, lunch is whatever fits between two slices of bread, and the commute is eleven minutes on a bicycle with a view of the sea that I have stopped noticing and should not have.

Lagos. I leave home at 5:30 to beat the traffic, because the same journey takes forty minutes then and two hours at seven. Work is 8 to 5 at a logistics company. Lunch is usually jollof rice or beans and plantain from the woman outside our gate, who knows everyone's order by heart.

I get home around 7:30 and CSS happens from nine to eleven, if there is power. If there isn't, I read on my phone and plan what to build tomorrow.

Night shift at a warehouse in a rainy northern city, which is why you see me posting at silly hours. Start at ten in the evening, finish at six, sleep until two, practise runs until dinner. My lunch is at 2 a.m. and it is always soup. Nobody should envy this schedule, but the roads are empty and the internet is fast.

Small request from someone who does everything with as few inputs as possible. On long threads I'd love to press `j` and `k` to jump to the next and previous post, and maybe `r` to start a reply to the one that is focused.

Is that something the new version can do already and I have missed it, or could it be added? I promise to stop asking for things after this one.

Not there yet, and it is a reasonable ask. I have added it to the list for the next update, with one condition from our side: shortcuts will be off while a text field has focus, so nobody replies by accident mid-sentence. No promise needed, keep the requests coming.

`strict` is a given. I mean the ones beyond it.

Mine, in every project:

- `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`: annoying for a week, then you stop writing bugs with arrays
- `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`: catches the difference between missing and undefined
- `noImplicitOverride`

I gave up on `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`. What is on your list?
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` everywhere, same as you. This forum's data layer is written with it on, and it caught two real bugs in the first week.
I only script spreadsheets, so take this lightly: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is the one that made me understand why my column lookups kept returning undefined.

> made me understand why my column lookups kept returning undefined

That is exactly the bug it exists for. A lookup that can miss should say so in its type.
As the person who only writes build scripts for icon sprites: I turned on `strict` once and was told about forty problems I did not know I had. Fixed them all. Still a little proud.
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is the one I switch off again in every codebase that talks to a third-party API. Worth it for your own types, painful at the boundary.
Agreed at the boundary. I parse at the edge and keep the strict types inside, so the flag only ever sees data I shaped myself.

Before any investing thread makes sense, there is this question. I keep six months of expenses in a boring savings account and do not touch it.

Eight months. Template income is lumpy: a good launch month can be followed by three quiet ones, and I sleep better with the extra cushion.
Freelancer here: six months, plus a separate pot for taxes. The tax pot is the one that actually saved me.
Salaried, three months. Reading this thread I am starting to think that is the optimistic end.
Three on a stable salary is defensible. The number matters less than having decided it before you need it.
Six, split over two banks. Not for the returns, just so a frozen card on a Friday evening is an inconvenience and not a crisis.

I have sold templates for a one-off price for two years. Every few months someone tells me I am leaving money on the table by not charging yearly.

My worry: a subscription means I owe people updates forever, and a template is supposed to be finished. Has anyone here switched, in either direction?
As a buyer: I avoid subscription templates. I want to pay once, own the files and never think about it again.
Run the numbers before the feelings. What share of buyers come back for a second template within a year? If it is under a third, a subscription mostly adds churn and support.
About a quarter come back. So by that rule the answer is no, which matches my gut. Thank you for making it a number.
A middle road I have seen work: one-off price, plus a paid major version every year or two. Nobody feels locked in and you still get paid for the big updates.
That is how I do the icon packs. Volume 1 owners get a discount on volume 2 and nobody has ever complained.
Same move two years ago. The hardest part was deleting the app that showed me the price every day.
Deleting the app is the real strategy. The fund is a detail.
Beginner question: is one fund really enough, or is that only fine once you know what you are doing?
It is the other way round. One broad fund is what you buy when you admit you do not know which part of the market will do well. That is everyone.
